one_liner: Learned monotone minimal perfect hash (key to sorted rank): about 3-5 bits/key and 7-18x faster queries than trie-based MMPHFs.
what_it_does: It is a monotone minimal perfect hash function (MMPHF). You build it once from a sorted, duplicate-free key set S, and it maps every key in S to its rank (0..n-1 in sorted order) without storing the keys. It uses about 2.6-4.9 bits/key for 64-bit integers and about 6-6.5 bits/key for strings. The API is a class template: construct `lemonhash::LeMonHash<> h(std::vector<uint64_t>)` or `lemonhash::LeMonHashVL<> h(std::vector<std::string>)`, and `h(key)` returns the rank as a size_t. Keys not in S get an arbitrary value. The structure is static (no insert or delete) and has no save/load API, so you rebuild it from the key vector every time.
how_it_is_fast: Trie-based MMPHFs walk a trie; LeMonHash instead learns the key distribution. A PGM-index (an error-bounded piecewise-linear model, epsilon=31 by default) gives each key an approximate rank, which is used directly as its bucket index, so most buckets hold 0 or 1 keys. The start rank of each bucket is kept as a unary bit vector with a pasta select structure (2n+o(n) bits). Only keys that collide get a local rank stored, in one of ten BuRR (bumped ribbon retrieval) structures picked by ceil(log2 bucket size); the paper puts BuRR's space overhead below 1%. A query is a predecessor search over the PGM segments, one linear-model evaluation, one select and at most one retrieval lookup. That is a small, flat number of memory accesses, where Hollow and ZFast tries chase pointers down O(log u) levels. LeMonHash-VL applies the same scheme recursively to strings. It strips each node's common prefix and turns the next 64-bit chunk into a key, compressing the chunk through a per-node reduced alphabet. It finds child nodes through a PTHash MPHF and per-level partitioned Elias-Fano offset arrays.
when_to_use: Static, sorted sets of 64-bit integers (IDs, positions, cell IDs, timestamps) where you need each key's rank but cannot afford to store the keys. The paper measured 2.6-3.0 bits/key on uniform, normal, exponential and 5gram data and 4.4-4.9 bits/key on osm and fb, against 4.1-5.6 bits/key for the Hollow-Trie family and 6.1-7.9 for PaCo and ZFast.

Query-heavy rank lookups on large sets (100M-800M keys). Single-threaded on a 2014 Xeon it answers 1.3-2.7M queries/s: about 7-8x the Grossi-Ottaviano C++ Hollow Trie and 12-18x the Sux4J Java tries, at the same or smaller space on every integer dataset except fb.

Mapping a sorted key universe onto a dense value array while keeping locality. Consecutive keys land in consecutive slots, so range scans stay sequential. The paper notes this can make an MMPHF preferable to a plain MPHF for array indexing, because memory accesses in sorted order are cache-friendlier.

Sorted string dictionaries (terms, k-mers) with LeMonHash-VL, when query speed matters more than the last 10-13% of space. On 35M web terms it answers 1.28M queries/s at 6.08 bits/key. The smallest competitor (HTDist) manages 0.09M/s at 5.40 bits/key, and the C++ Hollow Trie 0.35M/s at 5.84.

Batch rebuilds where construction time counts. The default epsilon=31 integer build runs at 5.0-8.5 MKeys/s single-threaded (about 120-200 ns/key), up to 2x faster than the competitor with the next-best space.
when_not_to_use: You do not need sorted order. Every catalogued sibling is a non-monotone MPHF at about 1.5-3 bits/key, with catalogued query times in the tens of nanoseconds (on other hardware). In the paper's runs LeMonHash takes about 370-750 ns per integer query and 0.8-3 us per string query.

Membership tests or changing key sets. Foreign keys get an arbitrary rank (there is no fingerprint), any insert means a full rebuild, and without serialization every process start rebuilds from the full in-memory key vector: 5-8.5 MKeys/s for integers, 2.3-2.7 MKeys/s for strings.

Long URL-like strings, or when minimum space is the goal. On 106M URLs (average 105 bytes) LeMonHash-VL drops to 338K queries/s, and the C++ Centroid Hollow Trie is 18% faster there (399K/s at 8.36 vs 6.46 bits/key). On strings, HTDist is 10-13% smaller. On fb IDs, the Hollow tries and HTDist beat LeMonHash's 4.91 bits/key (4.50-4.84).

Non-x86-64, non-GCC or non-Linux targets. support/util.h includes <immintrin.h> unconditionally, the string code assumes little-endian unaligned 64-bit loads, and CI covers only GCC 10-13 on x86-64 Ubuntu.
Proprietary or permissively licensed products. LeMonHash is GPL-3.0 and links GPL-3.0 ByteHamster/Util.

integration.form: header-only API (CMake INTERFACE target `LeMonHash`) that links small compiled shared libs: SimpleRibbon/BuRR, RibbonSorter and 4 sdsl-lite source files. It is consumed as a recursive git submodule via add_subdirectory; there are no install or package-config rules.
integration.dependencies: Git submodules: SimpleRibbon (Apache-2.0 BuRR wrapper, built as a shared lib, pulls ips2ra and tlx), ByteHamster/Util (GPL-3.0, pasta bit_vector, MurmurHash64), ds2i (partitioned Elias-Fano; its configuration.hpp uses boost::lexical_cast), sdsl-lite (bit utilities, partly compiled), PTHash (MIT, used by LeMonHash-VL for node lookup) and tlx. System: Boost (README requirement); CI also installs libtbb-dev. The PGM-index is re-implemented in-tree (include/bucket_mapping/support), not pulled as a dependency.
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (cxx_std_20) and CMake 3.25+. The README says GCC 11 or later, but the 2026-09-13 CI run built successfully on GCC 10, 11, 12 and 13. Clang and MSVC are not tested. The paper used GCC 11.1.0.
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux as written. The integer variant pulls in <immintrin.h> through BucketOffsets.hpp -> support/util.h. bextr uses BMI when __BMI__ is defined and falls back otherwise. ds2i is configured with SUCCINCT_USE_INTRINSICS, described as 'available on all x86-64'. -march=native is added only when LeMonHash is the top-level CMake project. The bundled benchmarks need glibc (mallinfo2). ARM, macOS and Windows are not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented, and operator() is non-const on every class. For integer LeMonHash the query path only reads: BucketOffsets::at and the PGM approximate_rank are const, and SimpleRibbon::retrieve is const, so concurrent queries through a shared non-const object look safe. LeMonHashVL is different: its query calls PartitionedEliasFano::at, which advances a ds2i enumerator stored as a member (move() writes m_position and the partition state). Concurrent queries on one LeMonHashVL object are therefore a data race; use one instance per thread or a lock. Construction is single-threaded.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it computes the same function (key -> rank in [0,n)) as the Sux4J and Grossi-Ottaviano MMPHFs, but as a C++ class built from a sorted std::vector<uint64_t> or std::vector<std::string>. It has no Java API, no transformation strategies for arbitrary key types and no serialization.

gotchas: Input must be sorted and duplicate-free, and the whole set must be in a std::vector. The integer constructor throws std::invalid_argument('Data not sorted or duplicates found'), but LeMonHashVL checks order only through debug asserts, so sort and deduplicate strings yourself.

Do not copy or move a built object. SimpleRibbon's MultiRetrievalDataStructure owns raw SimpleRibbon* pointers and deletes them in a user-declared destructor, with no copy or move constructors. The implicit copy (which a move also falls back to) therefore creates two owners, and both delete the same pointers. Construct in place or behind new/unique_ptr, as the author's MMPHF-Experiments wrapper does.

The defaults are the paper's tuned settings: LeMonHash<> uses SuccinctPGMBucketMapper<31>, and LeMonHashVL<> uses thresholds 128/128, alphabet reduction and UnalignedPGMBucketMapper<63>. epsilon=0 auto-tunes over 63/31/15 and roughly halves integer build speed (3.5 vs 6.5 MKeys/s on uniform keys) for little space gain. LinearBucketMapper and LeMonHashHeuristic only suit uniform data: on fb the linear mapper needs 34.35 bits/key and manages 0.8K queries/s.

LeMonHashVL packs a node's common-prefix length into a 15-bit field and per-level offset indexes into 30 bits, and throws 'Increase offsetsOffsetBits' when the offsets overflow. Expect trouble with shared prefixes over 32 KB or with more than about 1B bucket offsets in one tree level. spaceBits() prints to stdout.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: All catalogued siblings (PTHash, PtrHash, RecSplit, ShockHash, SicHash, PHast and others) are non-monotone MPHFs, so pick LeMonHash only when the output must be the key's rank in sorted order: range scans over a rank-indexed array, or rank queries on a static set without storing it. If any bijection to [0,n) will do, PTHash or PtrHash (about 3 bits/key and 37-45 ns queries in their entries) or ShockHash or RecSplit (1.56-1.8 bits/key) beat LeMonHash's 2.6-4.9 bits/key and roughly 0.37-0.75 us per integer query, though those numbers come from different hardware.
verified_claims_summary: The ESA 2023 paper (arXiv v3) ran single-threaded on an Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3 (2.3 GHz), with GCC 11.1.0 -O3 -march=native, and 5M random member queries per dataset. On 100M uniform 64-bit keys, LeMonHash (epsilon=31) answered 2.72M queries/s at 2.98 bits/key, against 0.35M at 4.61 for the Grossi-Ottaviano C++ Hollow Trie (7.7x) and 0.18M at 4.54 for Sux4J's Java Hollow Trie (15.2x). On 800M osm keys it answered 1.34M/s at 4.42 bits/key, against 0.073M for Sux4J's HTDist (18.3x) and 0.19M for the C++ Hollow Trie (7.2x). The Java baselines ran on OpenJDK 17 after one unmeasured JIT warm-up, each experiment ran twice and was averaged, and no std:: container, binary search or non-monotone MPHF was measured. The paper's own Table 2 reports 1.85M queries/s for the same uniform configuration, so per-query cost depends on the harness.
status_note: The code has barely changed since 2023: dependency and CMake upgrades in 2024-2025 and a BuRR submodule bump on 2026-09-13, with CI green on GCC 10-13. It has 32 stars and has never had an issue or PR filed. GPL-3.0 and the submodule-based build limit it to GPL-compatible projects.
